thread.title: PSG responds to letter asking provost to immediately resign - NewsBreak
thread.title_full: PSG responds to letter asking provost to immediately resign - NewsBreak

author: OLIVIA MAPES Editor-In-Chief
title: PSG responds to letter asking provost to immediately resign - NewsBreak
text:
By OLIVIA MAPES Editor-In-Chief ,
7 hours ago The Purdue Student Government has put out its official response to a group of faculty who wrote a letter calling for the immediate resignation of Provost Patrick Wolfe, and their list of 16 grievances explaining why the provost should step down.
In the letter, written by the Purdue chapter of American Association of University Professors, the provost is criticized for his unilateral decision making, including the nontransparent changes in the John Martinson Honors College, and for dean searches that have not been completed.
The statement written by PSG including— Rebecca Siener, the student body president, Nicholas Neuman, the student body vice president, and Launa Shaw, the student body secretary, among others, said it seconds many of the concerns brought up in the letter.
“PSG advocates for transparent and fair processes impacting educational attainment and quality for students,” PSG’s statement said. “Purdue prides itself on the quality of the education it provides, and students only receive such when faculty receive quality support and transparency on hiring, tenure, and academic freedom.”
The open letter from faculty said the university has had many top-down decisions without consulting with faculty.
“Meaningful consultation with established governance channels could mitigate unilateral decision-making,” PSG’s statement said. “While the Purdue Student Government recognizes the many external pressures placed on Purdue administration, transparency in decision-making and governance must improve.”
One of the issues outlined in AAUP’s letter was how the honors college was restructured, without any transparency or explanation on the process, leading to faculty losing their jobs without a backup or security plan.
PSG reaffirmed its support of the honors college, specifically its interdisciplinary nature.
“PSG has consistently expressed our support for diversity, equity, and inclusion on Purdue’s campus, despite recent changes. We remain committed to supporting all students of diverse backgrounds at both the undergraduate and graduate levels, and supporting the programming, faculty, and institutions meant to support their needs. PSG supports the John Martinson Honors College and has previously expressed our qualms about the University’s decision making in its restructuring. The academic freedom, initiatives, and opportunities this college provides to undergraduate Boilermakers is vital.”
PSG has started developing an honors transition team to help with the changes. They hope to keep the interdisciplinary nature of how the honors college was. The team meets with administrators letting them know what the student body wants.
“How we face that change (with the honors college) is important, whether or not we agree with it,” Siener said.
The letter from the faculty lists issues with transparency, dean searches, and an environment of self-censorship at Purdue.
Wolfe said upper-level decisions come with trade-offs, while the letter said Boilermakers across campus have lost confidence in Wolfe’s leadership.
“Though there are uncomfortable trade-offs required to be a leading public university, it becomes easier to move forward when underlying motives and external pressures shaping decisions are at least partially articulated," PSG's statement reads. "We believe improved institutional trust lies with utilization of the University Senate, Purdue Student Government Senate, and Purdue Graduate Student Government Senate as the advisory bodies they were designed to be.”
summary: In the letter, written by the Purdue chapter of American Association of University Professors, the provost is criticized for his unilateral decision making, including the nontransparent changes in the John Martinson Honors College, and for dean searches that have not been completed. “While the Purdue Student Government recognizes the many external pressures placed on Purdue administration, transparency in decision-making and governance must improve.” One of the issues outlined in AAUP’s letter was how the honors college was restructured, without any transparency or explanation on the process, leading to faculty losing their jobs without a backup or security plan.
